steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
On maps, the lighthouse was a small white dot staked to the edge of the world. On storm charts, it was a number and a name—North Grimness Light, Station 7. To Elias Moran, it was simply “the house.”

The house rose from the black rock like a tooth, five stories of whitewashed stone banded with rust from years of salt spray. It had a red cap, a glass eye, and a stairwell that coiled so sharply that when Elias climbed it too fast, his knees ached and his heart remembered that it was older than he wanted to think about.

He had been keeper for twenty-one years. Before him, there’d been a line of men whose faces stared from the gallery wall, each in the same heavy coat, each with the same squint that spoke of wind and glare. Elias sometimes felt only half-real without that coat, as if his identity began at the collar.

Every day held the same rhythm. Dawn meant inspecting the lens, clearing whatever salt the night had pinched into corners, checking the rotation gears, listening for any sound that didn’t belong: a grind where there should be a hum, a silence where something ought to click. Then weather readings sent by radio to the mainland. Then coffee, always too strong, in the kitchen that smelled faintly of oil and fish.

Out beyond the headland, the sea spread in every direction, a grey hide rippling and flexing with invisible muscle. On clear days, Elias could see the ferry’s white streak crossing towards the town, the gulls like confetti behind it. On fog days, everything vanished. The world became absence, the foghorn’s voice the only proof that anything remained beyond the rail.

Elias preferred the fog.

It suited the silence inside him.

He had not always lived alone. Before the lighthouse, there had been a small house on the hill overlooking the village. There had been a wife, Rowan, and a baby girl. The baby’s name was Cass; he rarely let himself say it aloud. Saying it made her real again, made the ache suddenly specific and sharp. Saying it meant remembering the last thing he saw of them: taillights disappearing into rain.

Rows of ships’ logs and maintenance charts lined his office, the neatness almost feverish. Between their dates and signatures, there was an absence—a period of five years when Station 7 had been automated. No keeper assigned, no handwriting, only printed maintenance reports from shore crews.

That blank span had covered his worst years. At the time, it felt like insult on top of injury, to lose not just his family but the house, the steady work that had kept him afloat. A budget line decided by someone who had never heard the hiss of oil lamps or felt the lens turn under their hand.

Technicians had come to “mothball” the station, disconnecting the living quarters from the main supply, installing sensors and remote controls. Elias had stood on the dock with his hands jammed in his coat pockets, watching the bulb blink under computer command, its slow rotation unmoored from any human touch.

“Progress,” they had said.

He had lasted two years down in town. He had tried shifts at the boatyard, odd jobs at the cannery, even a few weeks in the tourist center, repeating facts about the very lighthouse he’d loved: height in meters, year of construction, light’s visible range. His voice had sounded foreign, as if reading someone else’s memories from a script.

Sleep had shrunk to thin strips an hour long, easily torn. Some nights he drove along the clifftop road and parked where he could see the flash of the automatic light, regular as a heartbeat. He would sit in the dark, palms sweating on the steering wheel, and count: one, two, three… until the beam swept over him, through him, and then it would feel, for a second, as if someone had looked his way.

It was the shipwreck that changed things.

The “Freyja” went down on a black December night. An electronics failure, they said later, compounded by a freak squall. The automated systems worked; the log proved it. The light shone. The horn sounded. The charts were clear. And still, the Freyja slid onto an unremarkable spit of rock and opened her hull like a tin can.

Only four lives were lost. The rest clung to life rafts and were hauled in by the lifeboats during those impossible hours between three and five in the morning. But four was enough for the town to turn its gaze seaward with something like accusation. The news latched onto the story: “Lighthouse in Sight, Ship Still Strikes Rock. Is Automation to Blame?”

Elias didn’t know if having a keeper would have changed anything. Some wrecks were like that—stupid and inevitable, stitched into dark weather that left no room for grace. But he remembered the old days: the radio calls, the way a keeper could sense something wrong in the way the light of a ship moved, like a moth spiraling too near the flame. Sometimes a human eye caught what instruments didn’t. Sometimes a human voice, urgent and alive on the airwaves, cut through a captain’s pride.

There was a petition. The older fishermen signed first, their names looping and blotched. “Put a man back in the tower,” it read. “A real keeper.” Eventually the coastguard relented, part pilot program, part public relations. They needed someone who knew the station and the currents, who could manage old mechanisms alongside the new.

Elias did not need to be asked twice.

Now, three years back in the tower, his life had narrowed and steadied. The town was an occasional place—a supply run every fortnight, a drink at the pub where people nodded but did not intrude, then the familiar climb up the headland road until the lighthouse reared into view like the spine of some grounded whale.

He relished the routines. Rounding times were the bones of his day. He walked the gallery to check for cracked panes, tapped the old brass barometer in the hall, kept meticulous notes about birds on migration days. At night, he sat in the watch room with a mug of tea going cold by his elbow, the radar screen pulsing green at his shoulder, and listened to the soft tick of the lamp rotation.

Solitude was something he wore now as easily as his coat.

Still, the lighthouse was not quite as alone as it had used to be.

On his second spring back, a knock came at the door during a fog so dense it seemed the air itself had thickened. He almost didn’t hear it over the muffled boom of the horn. When he opened the door, a piece of the fog stepped in: a young woman, rain dripping from the hood of her parka, cheeks reddened from the climb.

“Afternoon,” she said, slightly breathless. “Sorry, I— Are you the keeper?”

Others had come before, of course. Day-trippers on clear weekends when the sea lay flat as glass. Curious tourists, hikers arriving with phones outstretched. Usually they stayed ten minutes, took a few photographs, and left with the sense that they had collected an old picturesque thing.

This woman was different. For one thing, she had come in the worst possible weather. For another, she had a notebook instead of a camera.

“I am,” he said.

“Good,” she replied, and smiled, quick and wary. “I’m June.”

She introduced herself as a researcher from the university. She was working on a project about lighthouse culture and the effects of automation on rural communities; she wanted to interview keepers, past and present.

“Past and present,” she repeated, glancing up the stairwell. “They said this station was manned again. I guessed you’d have seen both sides of it.”

Her voice carried an eagerness that made Elias instinctively defensive. He was used to the past being something to avoid, not excavate. But she waited, pen idle, making no assumption that he would say yes.

He let her in.

The interview began in the kitchen, over overboiled tea. She asked practical questions: routines, maintenance, interactions with passing vessels. Then came the thornier subjects—how it had felt when the station was automated. What people in the town had said. Whether he believed having a keeper now made a difference.

“I suppose I do,” he replied, and surprised himself with the firmness in his voice. “Else I wouldn’t be here.”

“And to you?” she asked.

“What about me?”

“What difference does it make to you, personally, to be back?”

He stared at the chipped rim of his mug. The hum of the generator, the faint rush of the sea against rock, the far-off moan of the foghorn—all the familiar sounds seemed to sharpen.

“It makes the days add up,” he said, at last. “When I was ashore, they didn’t. Here they… join into something. If I’m not here, and something happens, I’d know I should have been watching. It’s not…” He trailed off, shook his head. “It’s not rational. I know that. But that’s how it feels.”

She jotted something in her notebook, but her face had lost its interview intentness; she was just listening now.

“Did you always want to be a keeper?” she asked.

“Since I was small,” he said. “My grandfather did it. I’d sit in his kitchen and hear about ships swallowing the horizon like stars. Seemed like a kind of magic.”

“Still feel like magic?”

He considered the question. Outside, the fog pressed at the glass like a living thing.

“On certain nights,” he said quietly, “yeah.”

June came back twice more that summer, then once in autumn. The first time, she recorded their conversation on a small black device, asking about the Freyja and the petition that followed. The second time, the recorder stayed in her pocket, and they spent most of the visit in the lantern room while he pointed out distant navigation marks and the lanes the tankers preferred.

She was the one who noticed it first.

They were on the gallery walk, a band of wind-scoured steel encircling the lantern. The day was clear enough that the mainland loomed like a bruise on the horizon. June leaned on the rail, hair whipping, notebook tucked safely under her arm.

“Can I ask you something not for the project?” she said.

“You can ask.”

“Why does your log start again three years ago with a different hand?”

His fingers tightened on the rail. The question was casual in shape, but there was something gentle and deliberate beneath it.

“Different hand?” he repeated, playing for time.

“The old entries are loopier,” she said. “The new ones—yours—are… tighter? Smaller? I don’t know the right word. People change their handwriting when something big happens, my professor says. There’s a whole field about it.”

He thought of those blank years on the wall, the gap where there should have been ink and initials and weather records. His name had been neatly absent from the story of the station, as if he had stepped out of frame.

“Something big did happen,” he said. “Just… not to the lighthouse.”

He could have left it there. The wind tugged at his coat, flung itself in gusts against the tower. A cormorant arrowed past, black wings sharp against the sky.

He found himself talking.

Elias spoke haltingly at first, the facts pushed out like rusted bolts: the night of the crash, the call from the hospital, the rain on the road. June listened without interrupting, eyes mostly on the sea. He told her about the months after, when each day had been as featureless as unlit water. How he had drifted through jobs and rooms, unable to find a way for time to stick to him.

“I used to measure time by flashes,” he said. “By keeping the beam turning, making sure nothing broke the pattern. After the accident, I lost the… the timing of things. If that makes any sense.”

“It does,” June said.

“They automated the house that same year,” he went on. “Old budget was already in, decision made before the accident. But it felt like someone had taken a clock away from a man who’d just lost the last hour he really cared about.” He gave a brittle laugh. “It’s silly. The lighthouse isn’t alive. It didn’t know.”

June watched a wave slap itself into foam against a distant rock.

“Not silly,” she said. “Grief attaches itself where it can. Sometimes to places. Or work.”

“I used to think I watched ships,” Elias said. “Now I think I was watching for something else, without knowing it.”

They stood for a while in silence, the beam sweeping above them in its precise slow turn.

Later, when she had gone and the light had begun its evening pattern, Elias climbed into the lantern room alone and rested a hand on the cold girders. There were still computer panels here, shiny screens showing rotations per minute, energy draw, fault codes. The automation remained, humming and dutiful.

His hand slid from the metal to the brass plaque by the door, the one listing keepers’ names and dates of service. The old curator in town had added the latest line only last year:

E. Moran — Keeper — 2000–2010, 2023–

That thin dash between numbers, he thought, held an entire ocean’s worth of loss. Sandwiched between two spans of service, it looked almost neat. To anyone else it would be just a mark. To him it was every night he had waited in the dark for a light that did not bring anyone home.

He stayed there until dusk, watching the first stars fight their way through the sky’s haze. The light ignited with a soft electric click, flooding the glass with white.

From the outside, nothing had changed. The beam turned. The horn bellowed when fog crawled in. Ships passed, pilots checked their positions, captains muttered thanks or curses, radios crackled with terse words. The world used the light and rarely thought of the man who kept it.

Inside, in the narrow kitchen, a second chair began to gather use.

June’s visits became less about notes and more about cups of tea and borrowed books. She brought him a volume of poems about the sea, dog-eared and heavily underlined, and took away one of his grandfather’s logbooks, promising to return it unharmed. Sometimes she arrived with a bag of groceries, saying she had over-shopped by accident. Once she came in a gale so fierce the spray reached the top gallery, her cheeks bright, hair plastered to her forehead.

“Couldn’t stay in town,” she shouted over the wind. “Thought you might like someone to complain about the weather with.”

He did not say it aloud, but the sound of her boots on the metal steps, the sight of a second mug on the table, altered the shape of the house. Rooms that had felt like shells now held echoes of another breathing presence. It did not erase his grief, but it loosened its grip, made it share space with other, smaller concerns: whether the kettle would boil in time before the next hourly check, whether June would remember to duck in the low part of the stairwell, how many visits of hers he could reasonably expect before winter made the path too dangerous.

In the third year of his renewed tenure, another storm came.

It rolled in from the northeast, a bruised wall of cloud sweeping the sky clean of color. By afternoon the sea had climbed itself into wild, hollow-backed waves. Spray leapt the height of three men. The air was thick with spindrift, the horizon erased.

Elias went into storm routine without thinking. He checked the emergency generator, secured the shutters in the living quarters, confirmed radio channels with the coastguard. The light burned steady, its beam cutting a pale corridor through the dark, streaming rain.

Outside, the wind grew a voice. It howled down the chimney, flung itself bodily against the stone. The lighthouse shuddered, the old glass humming. Elias felt the familiar tension coiled between his shoulders, a tight wire he had carried since his very first storm. The sensation that this, now, mattered in a way that ordinary days did not.

Half past midnight, the radar pinged.

A green blot had appeared where there should have been none, ragged at the edges in the rain clutter but unmistakably moving. Small. Too close to the rocks. Elias leaned in, heart kicking.

“Small craft, what in God’s name are you doing out in this?” he muttered, then snapped the radio from its cradle.

He hailed on the emergency channel, voice level. “Unidentified vessel two miles northeast of North Grimness Light, this is North Grimness Station. You are heading into hazardous waters. Confirm your position.”

For a moment, only the broken static of storm answered. Then a thin voice came back, muffled and tense.

“North Grimness, this is the fishing vessel Larkspur. We’ve lost GPS and main engine. We’re trying to hold position, but we’re drifting.”

Elias pictured the map in his mind overlaying the radar screen. Larkspur. He knew the name—a small boat out of town, usually working crab pots close to shore.

“You’re thirty degrees off where you think you are,” he said, forcing calm into his words. “You’re coming down on the Black Sister rocks. Can you give me your compass heading and speed?”

The numbers came, stumbling. He scribbled them in grease pencil on the desk, did a quick calculation that was more instinct than math. The storm pushed from the northeast; the current ran hard here. The patterns were engraved in him the way others carried prayers.

“You need to turn twenty degrees to starboard,” he said. “Keep my light on your port side. I’m going to sound an additional pattern on the horn. Can you steer at all?”

“We’ve got emergency power to the rudder,” the voice said, strained. “Engine’s—” A sudden crash, a half-swallowed curse. “Wave just broke over the bow. We don’t know how long we can—”

“Listen to me,” Elias cut in, voice hard. “You keep my light where I tell you and I’ll keep you off the teeth. You’re closer than you think, but you’re not lost yet.”

He adjusted the foghorn, overlaying the standard pattern with a secondary blast—a code rarely used, an old system he and the other keepers had devised decades ago, back when not every situation fit neatly into the rulebooks. Short-short-long. Danger, alter course port.

He sent his own coordinates to the coastguard, relayed Larkspur’s estimated position. Their reply was terse: lifeboat launched, twenty minutes out. Twenty minutes could be an eternity in this sea, or no time at all.

The next ten minutes stretched and snapped, stretched and snapped. Elias held the radio tight enough to ache. Between transmissions, he watched the radar blot shift in slow, agonizing increments.

“Light’s on our port,” Larkspur’s skipper said. Elias could hear other voices behind him, shouting, swearing. “We can’t see the rocks.”

“You won’t,” Elias said. “Not until you hit them. Trust the radar and the horn. When I say now, you put her head into the waves as best you can and ride them. Don’t try and outrun them.”

He could
